acceptance_criteria.criterion: resolveCredential() returns the matching GitCredentialEntry when a valid credentialId is provided that matches an entry in the array.
resolveCredential() returns null when credentialId references a non-existent entry (stale reference).
resolveCredential() returns the single matching credential when the URL's host matches exactly one entry and no credentialId is provided (auto-selection).
resolveCredential() returns null when the URL's host matches zero entries and no credentialId is provided.
resolveCredential() returns null when the URL's host matches multiple entries and no credentialId is provided (ambiguous — requires user selection).
injectCredentialToken(url, token) injects the token as the WHATWG URL username into an HTTPS URL (same mechanism as the old injectCredentials()).
injectCredentialToken() returns the original URL unchanged for non-HTTPS URLs.

summary: Reviewed 2 files (src/git/git-credentials.ts, src/tests/git-credentials.test.ts). 0 Critical, 0 High, 1 Medium (noted), 2 Low (noted). Security sign-off: PASS. All OWASP Top 10 categories reviewed. No blocking findings.

comments.note: OWASP A02 (Cryptographic Failures) — INFO: Tokens (PATs) are stored as plain strings in GitCredentialEntry.token and in config.json on disk. config.ts applies chmod 0o600 to config.json on POSIX (confirmed in src/config/config.ts:218), which is a solid defence-in-depth control. No additional encryption-at-rest is applied, which is consistent with the threat model for a local developer tool. No finding — observed and confirmed acceptable.

OWASP A03 (Injection) — PASS: injectCredentialToken() and injectCredentials() both inject the token via WHATWG URL property assignment (parsed.username = token), NOT string concatenation. The WHATWG URL serialiser percent-encodes all special characters (@, /, #, etc.) automatically. This is confirmed safe and tested by an explicit test case for adversarially crafted tokens containing '@' and '/'. No injection vector identified.

OWASP A01 (Broken Access Control) — Medium / Informational: resolveCredential() with an explicit credentialId performs only an exact id match (credentials.find(c => c.id === credentialId)). There is no URL-host cross-validation when an explicit ID is supplied — i.e. a caller could pass credentialId='github-personal' but url='https://evil.com/repo.git' and receive the GitHub credential. The token is then passed to injectCredentialToken() and embedded in the URL to be used in the git operation. Risk depends entirely on caller discipline: if the URL has already been validated against the configured host at the call site (e.g. in the orchestrators), this is safe. Since WP-002 is a utility layer, and callers are not yet implemented (WP-005 updates call sites), this is noted as a design concern for the Reviewer and future orchestrator implementors to validate that host/credential coherence is enforced at the call site.

OWASP A09 (Security Logging & Monitoring) — Low: stripEmbeddedCredentials() is already implemented and available to sanitise URLs before they appear in logs or error messages. Correct use of this utility at all git operation call sites is important to prevent token leakage in logs. This concern is for the orchestrators (WP-005 scope), not WP-002 itself. WP-002 provides the sanitisation primitive; ensuring it is applied is a call-site responsibility.

OWASP A04/A07/A05/A06/A08/A10 — No issues identified. A04: No insecure defaults; null is returned for ambiguous or missing credential resolution. A07: No authentication/session logic in this module. A05: No configuration exposure. A06: No new third-party dependencies introduced — only Node.js built-in WHATWG URL API used. A08: No deserialization or build pipeline artefacts. A10: No server-side URL fetching; this module only manipulates URL strings.

comments.note: MAINTAINABILITY — No issues. All four functions are clearly named, single-responsibility, and fully documented with JSDoc (params, returns, security notes). The resolveCredential() implementation is admirably concise: the two-branch pattern (explicit-ID vs auto-selection) maps directly to the documented strategy. The short-circuit on host === null before filtering prevents a silent false-negative. Code is easy to reason about and modify.

BEST PRACTICES — WHATWG URL API is used correctly throughout: property assignment for token injection (not string concatenation), try/catch guarding every URL construction call, explicit parsed.password = '' to avoid residual password component. The ?? null idiom on Array.prototype.find is idiomatic TypeScript for converting undefined to null. Null-return for both zero-match and multi-match is the correct defensive default — forcing callers to handle the ambiguous case explicitly rather than silently using the wrong credential.

PERFORMANCE — No concerns. All operations are O(n) over the credential array (at most a few dozen entries in any realistic config). No unnecessary copies or repeated parsing. The early return pattern in extractHost() and injectCredentialToken() (check protocol before constructing second URL object) is efficient.

FUTURE CONTEXT — The dual-export of injectCredentials() + injectCredentialToken() is deliberately transitional (WP-005 will remove injectCredentials() call sites). This is acceptable as long as WP-005 actually removes the legacy function and its tests. The Developer's own debt comment in the implementation pipeline provides good tracking. No concern for this WP in isolation.

EDGE CASE — injectCredentialToken() uses extractHost() (which enforces https: protocol) as a guard, then immediately constructs a second new URL(url) in the try block. This is intentionally redundant — the second parse is needed to call .toString() — but it means two URL constructions per call. Acceptable at this scale; not a performance concern.

[documentation-forward] The module-level file comment for git-credentials.ts accurately states 'Only HTTPS URLs are supported' but does not mention the new resolveCredential() function or the resolveCredential → injectCredentialToken pipeline pattern. A short paragraph summarising the intended call sequence (resolveCredential() → entry.token → injectCredentialToken()) would help future contributors understand how the pieces compose, especially since injectCredentials() (legacy) and injectCredentialToken() (new) coexist in the same file.

[documentation-forward] The Security Auditor's Medium finding (OWASP A01: resolveCredential() with explicit credentialId does not cross-validate the URL host against the credential's configured host) is architecturally important for implementors of WP-005. This constraint should be documented either as a @remarks JSDoc block on resolveCredential() or as a dedicated SECURITY section in the module comment — whichever is more prominent. The note should state: 'When credentialId is supplied, the caller is responsible for ensuring the URL's host is consistent with the credential's configured host. No automatic cross-validation is performed.'
